title: Ἀμφὶ Σαρπηδόνα
titleEn: The Fight over Sarpedon’s Body — Iliad 16.569–675
source: Homer, The Iliad, Greek text of D. B. Monro and T. W. Allen, Homeri Opera, tomi I–II, 3rd ed. (Oxford Classical Texts; Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1920), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg001.perseus-grc2, sha256 ae8b617018c6e5af. Text as printed: the edition sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: The Trojans push the Achaeans back first: Hector strikes down Epeigeus, an exiled Myrmidon, with a rock, and Patroclus, angered, charges through the front line like a hawk and strikes Sthenelaus. The Trojans give way as far as a javelin flies, then Glaucus kills the Myrmidon Bathycles and Meriones kills Laogonus. Aeneas throws at Meriones and misses, and the two trade taunts until Patroclus rebukes Meriones: the fight will be won with hands, not words. Over Sarpedon’s body the din rises, and the dust and blood hide him. Zeus, watching, weighs whether Hector should kill Patroclus now, and chooses to let Patroclus drive the Trojans back; he puts fear into Hector, who flees in his chariot, and the Lycians flee too. The Achaeans strip Sarpedon of his armour, and Zeus tells Apollo to cleanse the body, wash and clothe it, and send it home to Lycia with Sleep and Death for burial.

sentences.t: ὦσαν δὲ πρότεροι Τρῶες ἑλίκωπας Ἀχαιούς·
sentences.tr: ōsan de proteroi Trōes helikōpas Achaious·
sentences.l: And pushed first the Trojans the quick-eyed Achaeans;
sentences.i: The Trojans were the first to push the quick-eyed Achaeans back;
sentences.n: The part opens in the fight over Sarpedon’s body, and the Trojans make the first push. ὦσαν is the aorist of ὠθέω ‘push’, and πρότεροι ‘first’ agrees with Τρῶες, ‘the Trojans first’. ἑλίκωπας, the masculine of the stock epithet ἑλικῶπις, is ‘quick-eyed’, a sense that is disputed. The next line, with γάρ, begins the explanation: an Achaean has just been hit. A new paragraph begins here.

sentences.t:
βλῆτο γὰρ οὔ τι κάκιστος ἀνὴρ μετὰ Μυρμιδόνεσσιν
υἱὸς Ἀγακλῆος μεγαθύμου δῖος Ἐπειγεύς,
ὅς ῥ’ ἐν Βουδείῳ εὖ ναιομένῳ ἤνασσε
τὸ πρίν·
sentences.tr:
blēto gar ou ti kakistos anēr meta Myrmidonessin
huios Agaklēos megathymou dios Epeigeus,
hos rh’ en Boudeiōi eu naiomenōi ēnasse
to prin·
sentences.i: For a man who was by no means the worst among the Myrmidons was struck: heavenly Epeigeus, son of great-hearted Agacles, who had ruled in well-peopled Budeion before;
sentences.n: γάρ gives the reason for the push: Epeigeus, a Myrmidon and so on Achilles’ side, has been hit. βλῆτο is the aorist passive of βάλλω ‘strike’ without the augment, and οὔ τι κάκιστος ‘by no means the worst’ understates, meaning a good man. Ἀγακλῆος is the genitive of Ἀγακλῆς, with the epic -ῆος for Attic -έους, and μεγαθύμου is ‘great-hearted’. ὅς ῥ’ is ὃς ῥα, ‘who’. ἤνασσε is the imperfect of ἀνάσσω ‘be lord, rule’, and ναιομένῳ is the participle of ναίω ‘dwell’ in the passive, ‘inhabited’. Budeion is a place this passage does not locate, and τὸ πρίν ‘formerly’ sets his rule against what the next lines say happened to him.

sentences.t:
ἀτὰρ τότε γ’ ἐσθλὸν ἀνεψιὸν ἐξεναρίξας
ἐς Πηλῆ’ ἱκέτευσε καὶ ἐς Θέτιν ἀργυρόπεζαν·
sentences.tr:
atar tote g’ esthlon anepsion exenarixas
es Pēlē’ hiketeuse kai es Thetin argyropezan·
sentences.l:
but then, a good cousin having despoiled,
to Peleus he supplicated and to Thetis, silver-footed;
sentences.i: but then, having killed a good cousin and stripped him of his armour, he made his plea as a suppliant to Peleus and to silver-footed Thetis;
sentences.n: Epeigeus’ story: he had to flee after a killing, and Peleus and Thetis took him in. ἀτὰρ τότε γε ‘but then’ sets this against his former rule. ἐξεναρίξας, the aorist participle of ἐξεναρίζω, is the verb for killing and stripping a victim, and the English gives both. ἀνεψιὸν ἐσθλόν is ‘a good cousin’. ἱκέτευσε is ‘made his plea as a suppliant’, with ἐς and the accusative, Πηλῆ’ being Πηλῆα elided. Θέτιν ἀργυρόπεζαν is ‘silver-footed Thetis’, her stock epithet.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ἅμ’ Ἀχιλλῆϊ ῥηξήνορι πέμπον ἕπεσθαι
Ἴλιον εἰς εὔπωλον, ἵνα Τρώεσσι μάχοιτο.
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ ham’ Achillēï rhēxēnori pempon hepesthai
Ilion eis eupōlon, hina Trōessi machoito.
sentences.l:
and they, together with Achilles, the man-breaker, sent him to follow
to Ilios of the fine foals, that with the Trojans he might fight.
sentences.i: and they sent him to follow with Achilles, the man-breaker, to Ilios of the fine foals, to fight the Trojans.
sentences.n: οἳ δ’ ‘and they’ are Peleus and Thetis, and the object ‘him’, Epeigeus, is left unsaid with πέμπον ‘were sending, sent’. ἅμ’ Ἀχιλλῆϊ ῥηξήνορι is ‘together with Achilles, the man-breaker’: Ἀχιλλῆϊ is the epic dative, and ῥηξήνωρ, from ῥήγνυμι ‘break’ and ἀνήρ ‘man’, leaves open whether ranks or men are broken. ἕπεσθαι is ‘to follow’. ἵνα with the optative μάχοιτο gives the purpose, ‘that he might fight’, Τρώεσσι being the epic dative plural. The second line is the Odyssey’s line (Agamemnon’s expedition) word for word.

sentences.t:
τόν ῥα τόθ’ ἁπτόμενον νέκυος βάλε φαίδιμος Ἕκτωρ
χερμαδίῳ κεφαλήν·
sentences.tr:
ton rha toth’ haptomenon nekyos bale phaidimos Hektōr
chermadiōi kephalēn·
sentences.l:
Him then, as he laid hold of the dead man, struck glorious Hector
with a rock on the head;
sentences.i: Glorious Hector struck him on the head with a rock as he laid hold of the dead man;
sentences.n: Hector is the striker and Epeigeus the man struck. τόν ῥα τόθ’ is ‘him then, at that moment’. ἁπτόμενον is the present participle of ἅπτομαι ‘lay hold of’, with the genitive νέκυος ‘of the dead man’; the dead man is not named in the line, but the whole fight is over Sarpedon (named at 638). βάλε takes two accusatives, the man (τόν) and the part struck (κεφαλήν ‘on the head’), and χερμαδίῳ is the dative of means, ‘with a rock’.

sentences.t:
ἣ δ’ ἄνδιχα πᾶσα κεάσθη
ἐν κόρυθι βριαρῇ·
sentences.tr:
hē d’ andicha pasa keasthē
en korythi briarēi·
sentences.l:
and it was split in two, the whole of it,
inside the weighty helmet;
sentences.i: and the whole head was split in two inside the heavy helmet;
sentences.n: ἣ is feminine and means the head, κεφαλήν of the line before. κεάσθη is the aorist passive of κεάζω ‘split’, and ἄνδιχα is ‘in two’, with πᾶσα ‘the whole of it’; the pair ἄνδιχα … κεάσθη stands also at 16.412. κόρυθι βριαρῇ is ‘in the weighty helmet’ (βριαρός, from βρίθω ‘be heavy’), as at 16.413; the head is split inside the helmet. The line is that of 16.412–413.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ ἄρα πρηνὴς ἐπὶ νεκρῷ
κάππεσεν, ἀμφὶ δέ μιν θάνατος χύτο θυμοραϊστής.
sentences.tr:
ho d’ ara prēnēs epi nekrōi
kappesen, amphi de min thanatos chyto thymoraïstēs.
sentences.l:
and he, face down, onto the corpse
fell down, and about him death was poured, life-destroying.
sentences.i: and he fell face down upon the corpse, and death, the destroyer of life, was poured about him.
sentences.n: Epeigeus falls on the body he had taken hold of. ὃ δ’ ἄρα is ‘and he’, πρηνής ‘face down’, and ἐπὶ νεκρῷ ‘upon the corpse’. κάππεσεν is κατέπεσεν, ‘fell down’, with the κατ- assimilated before π. ἀμφὶ … χύτο is split by tmesis, ‘was poured about’, from χέω. θάνατος θυμοραϊστής ‘death, the destroyer of life’ is the formula of 13.544 and 16.414; these two lines are those of 16.413–414, where the first has γαίῃ ‘earth’ in place of νεκρῷ.

sentences.t:
Πατρόκλῳ δ’ ἄρ’ ἄχος γένετο φθιμένου ἑτάροιο,
ἴθυσεν δὲ διὰ προμάχων ἴρηκι ἐοικὼς
ὠκέϊ, ὅς τ’ ἐφόβησε κολοιούς τε ψῆράς τε·
sentences.tr:
Patroklōi d’ ar’ achos geneto phthimenou hetaroio,
ithysen de dia promachōn irēki eoikōs
ōkeï, hos t’ ephobēse koloious te psēras te·
sentences.i: And grief came on Patroclus for his fallen companion, and he charged through the foremost fighters like a swift hawk that puts jackdaws and starlings to flight;
sentences.n: Patroclus turns from the stricken man to avenge him; the companion is Epeigeus. ἄχος γένετο is ‘grief came to be’ for Patroclus (dative), with φθιμένου ἑτάροιο ‘for the perished companion’ in the genitive. ἴθυσεν is the aorist of ἰθύω ‘charge straight’, and διὰ προμάχων is ‘through the front-fighters’. ἴρηκι ἐοικώς is ‘like a hawk’, and ὠκέϊ, the epic dative of ὠκύς, agrees with ἴρηκι. ὅς τ’ ἐφόβησε is an aorist in a comparison, which states what a hawk does in general (‘puts to flight’), τε marking the general statement. κολοιούς are ‘jackdaws’ and ψῆρας ‘starlings’, the usual identifications.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἰθὺς Λυκίων Πατρόκλεες ἱπποκέλευθε
ἔσσυο καὶ Τρώων, κεχόλωσο δὲ κῆρ ἑτάροιο.
sentences.tr:
hōs ithys Lykiōn Patroklees hippokeleuthe
essyo kai Trōōn, kecholōso de kēr hetaroio.
sentences.l:
so straight at the Lycians, Patroclus, horse-urging one,
you rushed, and the Trojans, for you were angered in heart for your companion.
sentences.i: So you rushed straight at the Lycians and the Trojans, Patroclus, you who urge horses on, for you were angered in heart over your companion.
sentences.n: The poet turns and speaks to Patroclus as ‘you’, a way he has of marking a man he pities or admires. ὣς answers the comparison of the hawk. ἰθύς ‘straight’ takes the genitives Λυκίων and Τρώων, ‘straight at the Lycians and the Trojans’. ἔσσυο is the second person of the aorist middle ἐσσύμην of σεύω ‘rush’. Πατρόκλεες ἱπποκέλευθε is the vocative, ‘Patroclus, horse-urging one’ (ἱπποκέλευθος, as at 16.126). κεχόλωσο is the second person of the pluperfect passive of χολόω ‘anger’, ‘you had been angered’, which stands for ‘you were angry’, with κῆρ ‘in heart’ as an accusative of respect and ἑτάροιο, the genitive of cause, ‘over your companion’.

sentences.t:
καί ῥ’ ἔβαλε Σθενέλαον Ἰθαιμένεος φίλον υἱὸν
αὐχένα χερμαδίῳ, ῥῆξεν δ’ ἀπὸ τοῖο τένοντας.
sentences.tr:
kai rh’ ebale Sthenelaon Ithaimeneos philon huion
auchena chermadiōi, rhēxen d’ apo toio tenontas.
sentences.l:
And he struck Sthenelaus, Ithaemenes’ dear son,
on the neck with a rock, and broke off from him the tendons.
sentences.i: And he struck Sthenelaus, the dear son of Ithaemenes, on the neck with a rock, and broke the tendons away from him.
sentences.n: The subject is Patroclus, who is again ‘he’. βάλε takes the man (Σθενέλαον) and the part struck (αὐχένα ‘the neck’) in the accusative, and χερμαδίῳ is ‘with a rock’. Ἰθαιμένεος is the epic genitive of Ἰθαιμένης. ῥῆξεν … ἀπό is split by tmesis, ‘broke off’, and τοῖο is the epic genitive of the demonstrative, ‘from him’. τένοντας are ‘tendons’, here those of the neck.

sentences.t: χώρησαν δ’ ὑπό τε πρόμαχοι καὶ φαίδιμος Ἕκτωρ.
sentences.tr: chōrēsan d’ hypo te promachoi kai phaidimos Hektōr.
sentences.l: And back gave way the front-fighters and glorious Hector;
sentences.i: Both the foremost fighters and glorious Hector gave way;
sentences.n: Struck, Sthenelaus’ side gives ground, Hector with them; the line is word for word 4.505. χώρησαν … ὑπό is split by tmesis (ὑποχωρέω ‘give way, withdraw’), the aorist of χωρέω ‘give way’. πρόμαχοι are ‘front-fighters’, and τε … καί pairs them with φαίδιμος Ἕκτωρ ‘glorious Hector’.

sentences.t:
ὅσση δ’ αἰγανέης ῥιπὴ ταναοῖο τέτυκται,
ἥν ῥά τ’ ἀνὴρ ἀφέῃ πειρώμενος ἢ ἐν ἀέθλῳ
ἠὲ καὶ ἐν πολέμῳ δηΐων ὕπο θυμοραϊστέων,
τόσσον ἐχώρησαν Τρῶες, ὤσαντο δ’ Ἀχαιοί.
sentences.tr:
hossē d’ aiganeēs rhipē tanaoio tetyktai,
hēn rha t’ anēr apheēi peirōmenos ē en aethlōi
ēe kai en polemōi dēïōn hypo thymoraïsteōn,
tosson echōrēsan Trōes, ōsanto d’ Achaioi.
sentences.l:
And as great as the rush of a javelin, long, is,
which a man may hurl, making trial, either in a contest
or even in war, beneath enemies life-destroying,
so far gave way the Trojans, and pushed-back the Achaeans.
sentences.i: As far as the rush of a long javelin carries, when a man hurls it in making trial, whether in a contest or even in war, under the pressure of life-destroying enemies, so far did the Trojans give way, and the Achaeans pushed them back.
sentences.n: The comparison measures how far the Trojans fell back: as far as a javelin flies when thrown to test its range, in a contest or in earnest. ὅσση … τόσσον is ‘as great as … so far’. αἰγανέης ταναοῖο is ‘of a long javelin’ (ταναός, from τανύω ‘stretch’), ῥιπή ‘rush’ is the force and flight of the throw, and τέτυκται, the perfect passive of τεύχω, serves as ‘is’. ἀφέῃ is a subjunctive of ἀφίημι ‘let go’, a general statement, and πειρώμενος, from πειράομαι, is ‘making trial’ with no object. ἐν ἀέθλῳ is ‘in a contest’. δηΐων ὕπο θυμοραϊστέων has ὕπο after its noun; δήϊοι ‘enemies’, and θυμοραϊστής ‘life-destroying’ is the adjective of 13.544. ἐχώρησαν is ‘gave way’, and ὤσαντο, the middle of ὠθέω, is ‘pushed back’ with the Trojans understood.

sentences.t:
Γλαῦκος δὲ πρῶτος Λυκίων ἀγὸς ἀσπιστάων
ἐτράπετ’, ἔκτεινεν δὲ Βαθυκλῆα μεγάθυμον
Χάλκωνος φίλον υἱόν, ὃς Ἑλλάδι οἰκία ναίων
ὄλβῳ τε πλούτῳ τε μετέπρεπε Μυρμιδόνεσσι.
sentences.tr:
Glaukos de prōtos Lykiōn agos aspistaōn
etrapet’, ekteinen de Bathyklēa megathymon
Chalkōnos philon huion, hos Helladi oikia naiōn
olbōi te ploutōi te meteprepe Myrmidonessi.
sentences.l:
And Glaucus, first, leader of the Lycians, the shield-bearers,
turned about, and killed Bathycles, great-hearted,
Chalcon’s dear son, who in Hellas, inhabiting a home,
in prosperity and wealth was conspicuous among the Myrmidons.
sentences.i: And Glaucus, the leader of the Lycian shield-bearers, was the first to turn round, and he killed great-hearted Bathycles, the dear son of Chalcon, who lived in a home in Hellas and was conspicuous among the Myrmidons for his prosperity and wealth.
sentences.n: Glaucus now strikes for the Lycians; Bathycles, a Myrmidon, is his victim. Λυκίων ἀγὸς ἀσπιστάων is ‘leader of the Lycians, the shield-bearers’, as at 16.490. ἐτράπετ’ is the aorist middle of τρέπω, ‘turned himself round’; 598 shows he turned on his pursuer. πρῶτος is ‘first’. Βαθυκλῆα is the accusative of Βαθυκλῆς, and Χάλκωνος φίλον υἱόν ‘the dear son of Chalcon’. Ἑλλάδι is Hellas, here a region of Achilles’ country, as at 2.683, not the whole of Greece. οἰκία ναίων is ‘inhabiting a home’; ὄλβῳ τε πλούτῳ τε is ‘in prosperity and in wealth’, and μετέπρεπε is ‘was conspicuous among’, with the dative Μυρμιδόνεσσι.

sentences.t:
τὸν μὲν ἄρα Γλαῦκος στῆθος μέσον οὔτασε δουρὶ
στρεφθεὶς ἐξαπίνης, ὅτε μιν κατέμαρπτε διώκων·
sentences.tr:
ton men ara Glaukos stēthos meson outase douri
strephtheis exapinēs, hote min katemarpte diōkōn·
sentences.l:
Him then Glaucus in the middle of the chest wounded with a spear,
having turned suddenly, when he was overtaking him, pursuing;
sentences.i: Glaucus stabbed him with a spear in the middle of the chest, turning suddenly as Bathycles, in pursuit, was overtaking him;
sentences.n: τὸν μὲν ἄρα ‘him then’ is Bathycles. The one who was overtaking is Bathycles, the one overtaken Glaucus (μιν); Glaucus turns and strikes. στρεφθείς is the aorist passive participle of στρέφω, ‘having turned round’. κατέμαρπτε is the imperfect of καταμάρπτω ‘overtake’, and διώκων ‘pursuing’. οὔτασε is the aorist of οὐτάω, a thrust from close at hand, and στῆθος μέσον is ‘the middle of the chest’, an accusative of the part struck.

sentences.t: δούπησεν δὲ πεσών·
sentences.tr: doupēsen de pesōn·
sentences.l: and he fell with a thud;
sentences.i: and he fell with a thud;
sentences.n: Bathycles falls. δούπησεν is the aorist of δουπέω ‘thud’, said of a heavy body falling, and πεσών is ‘having fallen’; the English gives the two together as ‘fell with a thud’. The same words close the death of a man in other parts.

sentences.t:
πυκινὸν δ’ ἄχος ἔλλαβ’ Ἀχαιούς,
ὡς ἔπεσ’ ἐσθλὸς ἀνήρ·
sentences.tr:
pykinon d’ achos ellab’ Achaious,
hōs epes’ esthlos anēr·
sentences.l:
and thick grief seized the Achaeans,
when fell the good man;
sentences.i: and thick grief seized the Achaeans as the good man fell;
sentences.n: The Achaeans’ grief at the fall of one of their own. πυκινόν is ‘thick, close-packed’, here of grief that closes in on them. ἔλλαβ’ is ἔλλαβε, the aorist of λαμβάνω ‘seize’, with the doubled λ. ὡς is ‘when, as’, and ἔπεσ’ is ἔπεσε ‘fell’. ἐσθλὸς ἀνήρ is ‘the good man’; ἐσθλός ‘good’ is a word of praise for a man in battle.

sentences.t:
μέγα δὲ Τρῶες κεχάροντο,
στὰν δ’ ἀμφ’ αὐτὸν ἰόντες ἀολλέες·
sentences.tr:
mega de Trōes kecharonto,
stan d’ amph’ auton iontes aollees·
sentences.l:
and greatly the Trojans rejoiced,
and stood about him, going, in a close mass;
sentences.i: and the Trojans rejoiced greatly, and went and stood around him in a close mass;
sentences.n: The Trojans’ answer: gladness, and a close ring round the fallen man. μέγα ‘greatly’ is an adverb, and κεχάροντο is a reduplicated aorist of χαίρω ‘rejoice’. στάν is the unaugmented plural aorist of ἵστημι (= ἔσταν), ‘stood’, and ἰόντες ‘going’ adds that they went and stood. ἀμφ’ αὐτόν is ‘around him’, and ἀολλέες ‘in a close mass’ describes the Trojans together.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ἄρ’ Ἀχαιοὶ
ἀλκῆς ἐξελάθοντο, μένος δ’ ἰθὺς φέρον αὐτῶν.
sentences.tr:
oud’ ar’ Achaioi
alkēs exelathonto, menos d’ ithys pheron autōn.
sentences.l:
Nor then did the Achaeans
forget their might, and their might straight on they bore, their own.
sentences.i: Nor did the Achaeans forget their might, but kept carrying their own might straight on.
sentences.n: The Achaeans do not give way. οὐδ’ ἄρ’ is ‘nor then’. ἐξελάθοντο is the aorist middle of ἐκλανθάνομαι ‘forget’, which takes the genitive ἀλκῆς (ἀλκή ‘might’). μένος ‘might’ is the object of φέρον, the imperfect, ‘were carrying’, and αὐτῶν, the genitive of αὐτός, makes it ‘their own’. ἰθύς is ‘straight’. Both ἀλκή and μένος are ‘might’ in this series, so the English repeats the word.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ αὖ Μηριόνης Τρώων ἕλεν ἄνδρα κορυστὴν
Λαόγονον θρασὺν υἱὸν Ὀνήτορος, ὃς Διὸς ἱρεὺς
Ἰδαίου ἐτέτυκτο, θεὸς δ’ ὣς τίετο δήμῳ.
sentences.tr:
enth’ au Mērionēs Trōōn helen andra korystēn
Laogonon thrasyn huion Onētoros, hos Dios hireus
Idaiou etetykto, theos d’ hōs tieto dēmōi.
sentences.l:
Then in turn Meriones of the Trojans took a helmeted warrior,
Laogonus, the bold son of Onetor, who of Zeus the priest
of Ida had been made, and like a god was honoured in the land.
sentences.i: Then in turn Meriones killed a helmeted warrior of the Trojans, Laogonus, the bold son of Onetor, who had been made priest of Idaean Zeus and was honoured like a god in the land.
sentences.n: Meriones’ kill. ἔνθ’ αὖ is ‘then in turn’, and Τρώων ἕλεν ἄνδρα ‘took a man of the Trojans’ means killed him: ἕλεν is the unaugmented aorist of αἱρέω. κορυστής, built on κόρυς ‘helmet’ and κορύσσω ‘arm’, is ‘helmeted warrior’, ‘armed man’ being the other reading. θρασύς is ‘bold’. ἱρεύς is ἱερεύς ‘priest’, and Ἰδαίου ‘of Ida’, the Trojan mountain, an epithet of Zeus. ἐτέτυκτο is the pluperfect passive of τεύχω, ‘had been made’. θεὸς δ’ ὣς τίετο δήμῳ ‘was honoured like a god in the land’ is the half-line of 5.78, τίετο being the imperfect passive of τίω ‘honour’.

sentences.t:
τὸν βάλ’ ὑπὸ γναθμοῖο καὶ οὔατος· ὦκα δὲ θυμὸς
ᾤχετ’ ἀπὸ μελέων, στυγερὸς δ’ ἄρα μιν σκότος εἷλεν.
sentences.tr:
ton bal’ hypo gnathmoio kai ouatos· ōka de thymos
ōichet’ apo meleōn, stygeros d’ ara min skotos heilen.
sentences.l:
Him he struck beneath the jaw and the ear; and quickly the spirit
went from his limbs, and hateful darkness then seized him.
sentences.i: Meriones hit him beneath the jaw and the ear, and quickly his spirit left his limbs, and hateful darkness seized him.
sentences.n: The subject is Meriones; the weapon is not named. βάλ’ is βάλε, the unaugmented aorist of βάλλω. ὑπὸ γναθμοῖο καὶ οὔατος is ‘beneath the jaw and the ear’ (γναθμός ‘jaw’, οὔατος the epic genitive of οὖς), the words of 13.671. Laogonus dies at once, in the usual terms: the spirit (θυμός) leaves the limbs and darkness takes the dead man. ᾤχετ’ is ᾤχετο, the imperfect of οἴχομαι ‘be gone’, and μελέων is the uncontracted genitive plural of μέλος ‘limb’. στυγερὸς σκότος is ‘hateful darkness’, and εἷλεν is the aorist of αἱρέω ‘seize’. The two lines are those of 13.671–672.

sentences.t: Αἰνείας δ’ ἐπὶ Μηριόνῃ δόρυ χάλκεον ἧκεν·
sentences.tr: Aineias d’ epi Mērionēi dory chalkeon hēken·
sentences.l: And Aeneas at Meriones a bronze spear sent;
sentences.i: And Aeneas hurled a bronze spear at Meriones;
sentences.n: Aeneas answers at once. ἐπὶ Μηριόνῃ is ‘at Meriones’, ἐπί with the dative; χάλκεον is ‘of bronze’; and ἧκεν is the aorist of ἵημι ‘send, hurl’.

sentences.t: ἔλπετο γὰρ τεύξεσθαι ὑπασπίδια προβιβῶντος.
sentences.tr: elpeto gar teuxesthai hypaspidia probibōntos.
sentences.l: for he hoped to hit him, under the shield striding forward.
sentences.i: for he hoped to hit him as he strode forward under his shield.
sentences.n: Why Aeneas threw: he thought he could hit Meriones as he came on. ἔλπετο is the imperfect of ἔλπομαι ‘hope’. τεύξεσθαι is the future infinitive of τυγχάνω ‘hit’, which takes the genitive of the person hit, Meriones understood, and that is why προβιβῶντος ‘striding forward’ is also genitive. ὑπασπίδια is an adverb, ‘under the shield’, as at 13.158.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ὃ μὲν ἄντα ἰδὼν ἠλεύατο χάλκεον ἔγχος·
sentences.tr: all’ ho men anta idōn ēleuato chalkeon enchos·
sentences.l: But he, looking straight at it, avoided the bronze spear;
sentences.i: But Meriones, seeing it coming straight at him, avoided the bronze spear;
sentences.n: Meriones is the ‘he’ (ὃ μέν). ἄντα ἰδών is ‘looking straight at it’, and ἠλεύατο the aorist middle of ἀλέομαι ‘avoid’. The same line stands at 13.184, 13.404 and 13.503, said of other men.

sentences.t:
πρόσσω γὰρ κατέκυψε, τὸ δ’ ἐξόπιθεν δόρυ μακρὸν
οὔδει ἐνισκίμφθη, ἐπὶ δ’ οὐρίαχος πελεμίχθη
ἔγχεος·
sentences.tr:
prossō gar katekypse, to d’ exopithen dory makron
oudei eniskimphthē, epi d’ ouriachos pelemichthē
encheos·
sentences.i: for he bent forward, and the long spear behind him was fixed in the ground, and the butt-end of the spear shook;
sentences.n: How he escaped: he bent forward, and the spear stuck in the earth behind him. πρόσσω is ‘forward’, κατέκυψε the aorist of κατακύπτω ‘bend down’. τὸ … δόρυ μακρόν is ‘that long spear’, ἐξόπιθεν ‘from behind’, and ἐνισκίμφθη the aorist passive of ἐνισκίμπτω ‘fix in’, with the dative οὔδει ‘in the ground’. ἐπί is an adverb, ‘upon it’. οὐρίαχος is the butt-end of the spear, the spiked end opposite the point (the word of 13.443), and πελεμίχθη the aorist passive of πελεμίζω ‘shake’: the butt-end shakes as the head sticks in the ground.

sentences.t: ἔνθα δ’ ἔπειτ’ ἀφίει μένος ὄβριμος Ἄρης.
sentences.tr: entha d’ epeit’ aphiei menos obrimos Arēs.
sentences.l: and there then was letting go the might mighty Ares;
sentences.i: and then mighty Ares let the might go;
sentences.n: Whose might Ares lets go is not said. ἀφίει is the imperfect of ἀφίημι ‘let go, release’, and μένος has no possessive in the Greek, so both layers leave it open; the line follows the spent spear, and ‘its’ might is the natural sense, but the Greek does not say. The English is that of the same line at 13.444, where the word is ‘might’. ἔνθα … ἔπειτα is ‘there, then’, and ὄβριμος ‘mighty’ is Ares’ stock epithet.

sentences.t:
αἰχμὴ δ’ Αἰνείαο κραδαινομένη κατὰ γαίης
ᾤχετ’, ἐπεί ῥ’ ἅλιον στιβαρῆς ἀπὸ χειρὸς ὄρουσεν.
sentences.tr:
aichmē d’ Aineiao kradainomenē kata gaiēs
ōichet’, epei rh’ halion stibarēs apo cheiros orousen.
sentences.l:
And the point of Aeneas, quivering, into the earth
went off, since in vain from his stout hand it had darted.
sentences.i: And the point of Aeneas’ spear went off, quivering, into the ground, since it had sped in vain from his stout hand.
sentences.n: The cast is wasted. αἰχμή ‘point’ stands for the whole spear, κραδαινομένη is ‘quivering’, and κατὰ γαίης is ‘into the earth’, κατά with the genitive. ᾤχετ’ is ‘went off’. ἐπεί ῥ’ is ἐπεὶ ῥα ‘since’, ἅλιον ‘in vain’ is adverbial, and στιβαρῆς is ‘stout’. ὄρουσεν is ‘darted’. The same two lines tell, at 13.504–505, of Idomeneus’ escape from an earlier cast of Aeneas’.

sentences.t: Αἰνείας δ’ ἄρα θυμὸν ἐχώσατο φώνησέν τε·
sentences.tr: Aineias d’ ara thymon echōsato phōnēsen te·
sentences.l: And Aeneas then in spirit was incensed, and spoke:
sentences.i: Aeneas was incensed in his spirit, and spoke:
sentences.n: The words that follow are a taunt. ἐχώσατο is the aorist of χώομαι ‘be incensed’, with θυμόν ‘in spirit’ as an accusative of respect. φώνησε is the aorist of φωνέω ‘speak’, and the τε after it joins it to ἐχώσατο.

sentences.t:
Μηριόνη τάχα κέν σε καὶ ὀρχηστήν περ ἐόντα
ἔγχος ἐμὸν κατέπαυσε διαμπερές, εἴ σ’ ἔβαλόν περ.
sentences.tr:
Mērionē tacha ken se kai orchēstēn per eonta
enchos emon katepause diamperes, ei s’ ebalon per.
sentences.l:
“Meriones, very soon you, dancer though you are,
my spear would have stopped completely, if I had but hit you.”
sentences.i: “Meriones, dancer though you are, my spear would very soon have put a stop to you for good, if I had hit you.”
sentences.n: Aeneas jibes at Meriones for the nimble way he has just dodged: the dancer is not safe from a spear that hits. The condition is contrary to fact, εἰ with the aorist ἔβαλον ‘if I had hit’, answered by κεν with the aorist κατέπαυσε ‘would have stopped’ (καταπαύω ‘make stop’). τάχα κεν is ‘very soon’. καὶ ὀρχηστήν περ ἐόντα is ‘though you are a dancer’ (καὶ … περ marks the concession), ὀρχηστής being the noun behind ὀρχηστύς ‘dancing’. περ in εἴ σ’ ἔβαλόν περ is ‘but’, as if to say ‘had I only hit’. διαμπερές, ‘right through’, here ‘completely, for good’.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖ Μηριόνης δουρικλυτὸς ἀντίον ηὔδα·
sentences.tr: ton d’ au Mērionēs douriklytos antion ēuda·
sentences.l: To him in turn Meriones, famed-for-the-spear, spoke, face to face:
sentences.i: Then Meriones, famed for his spear, spoke to him in turn, face to face:
sentences.n: A new paragraph, and Meriones answers Aeneas. This is the reply-formula, with the name and epithet changed. δουρικλυτός is ‘famed for the spear’ (δόρυ and κλυτός), ἀντίον is ‘face to face’, and ηὔδα the imperfect of αὐδάω ‘speak’.

sentences.t:
Αἰνεία χαλεπόν σε καὶ ἴφθιμόν περ ἐόντα
πάντων ἀνθρώπων σβέσσαι μένος, ὅς κέ σευ ἄντα
ἔλθῃ ἀμυνόμενος·
sentences.tr:
Aineia chalepon se kai iphthimon per eonta
pantōn anthrōpōn sbessai menos, hos ke seu anta
elthēi amynomenos·
sentences.i: “Aeneas, mighty though you are, it is hard for you to quench the might of any man who comes against you in his own defence;
sentences.n: Meriones does not argue the dodge; he says that no man, however strong, can put out the might of every opponent. No verb is expressed with χαλεπόν, ‘hard’, which stands for ‘it is hard’. σε is the accusative subject of the infinitive σβέσσαι, the aorist infinitive of σβέννυμι ‘quench’, and καὶ ἴφθιμόν περ ἐόντα is ‘even though being mighty’. ὅς κέ … ἔλθῃ is a general ‘whoever may come’, with σευ the epic genitive of σύ and ἄντα ‘against’. ἀμυνόμενος is ‘defending himself’, from the middle of ἀμύνω.

sentences.t: θνητὸς δέ νυ καὶ σὺ τέτυξαι.
sentences.tr: thnētos de ny kai sy tetyxai.
sentences.l: and mortal, now, you too have been made.
sentences.i: and you too are mortal.
sentences.n: Aeneas is as killable as anyone. τέτυξαι is the second person of the perfect passive of τεύχω, ‘you have been made’, which serves as ‘you are’; θνητός is ‘mortal’, καὶ σύ ‘you too’, and νυ the particle ‘now, then’.

sentences.t:
εἰ καὶ ἐγώ σε βάλοιμι τυχὼν μέσον ὀξέϊ χαλκῷ,
αἶψά κε καὶ κρατερός περ ἐὼν καὶ χερσὶ πεποιθὼς
εὖχος ἐμοὶ δοίης, ψυχὴν δ’ Ἄϊδι κλυτοπώλῳ.
sentences.tr:
ei kai egō se baloimi tychōn meson oxeï chalkōi,
aipsa ke kai krateros per eōn kai chersi pepoithōs
euchos emoi doiēs, psychēn d’ Aïdi klytopōlōi.
sentences.l:
If even I should strike you, hitting you in the middle with sharp bronze,
quickly, strong though being and in your hands trusting,
a boast to me you would give, and your soul to Hades of the famous horses.”
sentences.i: If I too should strike you, hitting you in the middle with sharp bronze, then, strong though you are and trusting in your hands, you would quickly give me the triumph, and your soul to Hades of the famous horses.”
sentences.n: The other side of Aeneas’ taunt: the stronger man can be killed by a lesser. εἰ with the optative βάλοιμι ‘should I strike’ is answered by κε with the optative δοίης ‘you would give’; καὶ ἐγώ is ‘even I’. τυχών, the aorist participle of τυγχάνω, is ‘hitting’, with μέσον ‘in the middle’ and ὀξέϊ χαλκῷ ‘with sharp bronze’. αἶψα is ‘quickly’. κρατερός περ ἐών is ‘though being strong’, and χερσὶ πεποιθώς, from the perfect participle of πείθομαι, ‘trusting in your hands’. εὖχος … δοίης, ψυχὴν δ’ Ἄϊδι κλυτοπώλῳ echoes the pair of 5.654 (εὖχος ἐμοὶ δώσειν, ψυχὴν δ’ Ἄϊδι κλυτοπώλῳ), with the verb understood for the soul; the reason for Hades’ epithet κλυτόπωλος ‘of the famous horses’ is not known.

sentences.t: ὣς φάτο, τὸν δ’ ἐνένιπε Μενοιτίου ἄλκιμος υἱός·
sentences.tr: hōs phato, ton d’ enenipe Menoitiou alkimos huios·
sentences.l: So he spoke, and him rebuked Menoetius’ sturdy son:
sentences.i: So he spoke, and Menoetius’ sturdy son rebuked him:
sentences.n: A new paragraph: Patroclus, who is named only by his father, answers Meriones with a rebuke. ὣς φάτο is the unaugmented ‘so he spoke’, and ἐνένιπε the aorist of ἐνίπτω ‘rebuke’. Μενοιτίου ἄλκιμος υἱός is ‘Menoetius’ sturdy son’, ἄλκιμος coming from ἀλκή ‘might’.

sentences.t: Μηριόνη τί σὺ ταῦτα καὶ ἐσθλὸς ἐὼν ἀγορεύεις;
sentences.tr: Mērionē ti sy tauta kai esthlos eōn agoreueis;
sentences.l: “Meriones, why do you these things, though good being, say?
sentences.i: “Meriones, why do you, a good man, say these things?
sentences.n: Patroclus starts with the rebuke: a good man should not talk so. τί … ἀγορεύεις is ‘why do you say’, ταῦτα ‘these things’, and καὶ ἐσθλὸς ἐών ‘though being good’, with καί in the sense ‘even’.

sentences.t:
ὦ πέπον οὔ τοι Τρῶες ὀνειδείοις ἐπέεσσι
νεκροῦ χωρήσουσι·
sentences.tr:
ō pepon ou toi Trōes oneideiois epeessi
nekrou chōrēsousi·
sentences.l:
O good one, not indeed will the Trojans, by reproachful words,
from the dead body give way;
sentences.i: My good fellow, the Trojans will not give way from the dead body for words of reproach;
sentences.n: Words will not move the Trojans from the body. ὦ πέπον is a familiar address, ‘my good fellow’, and what πέπον originally means is not known. οὔ τοι is ‘not indeed’. ὀνειδείοις ἐπέεσσι is ‘with reproachful words’ (ὀνείδειος, from ὄνειδος ‘reproach’; ἔπος ‘word’, epic dative plural). χωρήσουσι is the future of χωρέω ‘give way’, with νεκροῦ in the genitive of separation, ‘from the dead body’.

sentences.t: πάρος τινὰ γαῖα καθέξει.
sentences.tr: paros tina gaia kathexei.
sentences.l: before that, someone the earth will hold down.
sentences.i: before that, the earth will hold someone fast.
sentences.n: They will not give way until men have died: the earth will take hold of someone first. πάρος is ‘before, sooner’, τινά ‘someone’, and καθέξει the future of κατέχω ‘hold down, hold fast’.

sentences.t: ἐν γὰρ χερσὶ τέλος πολέμου, ἐπέων δ’ ἐνὶ βουλῇ·
sentences.tr: en gar chersi telos polemou, epeōn d’ eni boulēi·
sentences.l: for in hands the end of war, and of words in counsel;
sentences.i: for the end of war is in the hands, and that of words in counsel;
sentences.n: No verb is expressed: ‘the end of war (is) in hands, (the end) of words in counsel’. τέλος is ‘end’ in the sense of what settles a matter; ἐν χερσί is ‘in hands’ and ἐνὶ βουλῇ ‘in counsel’, ἐνί being poetic ἐν. The two halves set fighting against talking.

sentences.t: τὼ οὔ τι χρὴ μῦθον ὀφέλλειν, ἀλλὰ μάχεσθαι.
sentences.tr: tō ou ti chrē mython ophellein, alla machesthai.
sentences.l: therefore not at all must one increase talk, but fight.”
sentences.i: So there is no need to increase talk: we must fight.”
sentences.n: Patroclus’ conclusion. τώ is ‘therefore’ (Attic τῷ). χρή takes the infinitives ὀφέλλειν and μάχεσθαι, ‘one must … increase … fight’, with οὔ τι ‘not at all’. ὀφέλλειν is ‘increase’ (ὀφέλλω, kept apart from ὀφείλω ‘ought’), with μῦθον ‘talk’. The speech ends.

sentences.t: ὣς εἰπὼν ὃ μὲν ἦρχ’, ὃ δ’ ἅμ’ ἕσπετο ἰσόθεος φώς.
sentences.tr: hōs eipōn ho men ērch’, ho d’ ham’ hespeto isotheos phōs.
sentences.l: So having spoken, the one led the way, and the other followed along, a man equal to a god.
sentences.i: So he spoke and led the way, and the other followed with him, a man the equal of a god.
sentences.n: A new paragraph: Patroclus leads, Meriones follows. ὃ μὲν … ὃ δέ is ‘the one … the other’, ἦρχ’ is the imperfect of ἄρχω ‘lead the way’, and ἕσπετο ‘followed’ goes with ἅμα ‘along with’. ἰσόθεος φώς ‘a man equal to a god’ is the stock phrase, here of Meriones, the second man (ὃ δ’).

sentences.t:
τῶν δ’ ὥς τε δρυτόμων ἀνδρῶν ὀρυμαγδὸς ὀρώρει
οὔρεος ἐν βήσσῃς, ἕκαθεν δέ τε γίγνετ’ ἀκουή,
ὣς τῶν ὄρνυτο δοῦπος ἀπὸ χθονὸς εὐρυοδείης
χαλκοῦ τε ῥινοῦ τε βοῶν τ’ εὐποιητάων,
νυσσομένων ξίφεσίν τε καὶ ἔγχεσιν ἀμφιγύοισιν.
sentences.tr:
tōn d’ hōs te drytomōn andrōn orymagdos orōrei
oureos en bēssēis, hekathen de te gignet’ akouē,
hōs tōn ornyto doupos apo chthonos euryodeiēs
chalkou te rhinou te boōn t’ eupoiētaōn,
nyssomenōn xiphesin te kai enchesin amphigyoisin.
sentences.l:
And of them, as of woodcutting men a din had arisen
in the glens of a mountain, and from afar comes the hearing of it,
so of them rose the thud from the wide-wayed earth
of bronze and of hide and of oxen, well-made,
being stabbed with swords and with double-pointed spears.
sentences.i: And as the din of woodcutters rises in the glens of a mountain and is heard from far off, so the thud of those men rose from the wide-wayed earth, of bronze and hide and well-made ox-hides, as they were stabbed with swords and double-pointed spears.
sentences.n: A comparison: the noise of the fighting is like woodcutters at work in the mountains, heard a long way off. The first τῶν ‘of them’ opens the comparison and the second (ὣς τῶν) resumes it; the English folds the pair into ‘those men’. ὥς τε is ‘as’, δρυτόμων ἀνδρῶν ‘woodcutting men’, and ὀρυμαγδός ‘a din’; ὀρώρει is a pluperfect, ‘had arisen’, used for a general statement. βήσσῃς is the epic dative plural of βῆσσα ‘glen’. ἀκουή is ‘hearing’, and ἕκαθεν ‘from afar’. ὄρνυτο is the imperfect middle of ὄρνυμι ‘rise’, δοῦπος ‘thud’, and εὐρυοδείης ‘wide-wayed’. ῥινοῦ ‘hide’ and βοῶν ‘oxen’ name shields by their covering. νυσσομένων is the genitive plural participle of νύσσω ‘stab’, agreeing with τῶν.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ἂν ἔτι φράδμων περ ἀνὴρ Σαρπηδόνα δῖον
ἔγνω, ἐπεὶ βελέεσσι καὶ αἵματι καὶ κονίῃσιν
ἐκ κεφαλῆς εἴλυτο διαμπερὲς ἐς πόδας ἄκρους.
sentences.tr:
oud’ an eti phradmōn per anēr Sarpēdona dion
egnō, epei beleessi kai haimati kai koniēisin
ek kephalēs eilyto diamperes es podas akrous.
sentences.l:
Not any longer even a shrewd man heavenly Sarpedon
would have recognised, for with missiles and blood and dust
from the head right through to the tips of his feet he was wrapped.
sentences.i: Not even a shrewd man could any longer have recognised heavenly Sarpedon, for he was wrapped in missiles, blood and dust from his head right down to the tips of his feet.
sentences.n: Sarpedon is named here for the first time in the part, as the body the fight is over. οὐδ’ ἂν … ἔγνω is ‘would not have recognised’ (the aorist of γιγνώσκω with ἄν), and ἔτι ‘any longer’. φράδμων is ‘shrewd, knowing’, with περ ‘even’. βελέεσσι is the epic dative plural, ‘with missiles’, and κονίῃσιν ‘in dust’. εἴλυτο is the pluperfect passive of εἰλύω ‘wrap’, ‘was wrapped’. ἐκ κεφαλῆς … ἐς πόδας ἄκρους is ‘from the head to the tips of the feet’, and διαμπερές ‘right through’.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ αἰεὶ περὶ νεκρὸν ὁμίλεον, ὡς ὅτε μυῖαι
σταθμῷ ἔνι βρομέωσι περιγλαγέας κατὰ πέλλας
ὥρῃ ἐν εἰαρινῇ, ὅτε τε γλάγος ἄγγεα δεύει·
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ aiei peri nekron homileon, hōs hote muiai
stathmōi eni bromeōsi periglageas kata pellas
hōrēi en eiarinēi, hote te glagos angea deuei·
sentences.i: And they kept thronging about the corpse without end, as when flies buzz about the pails brimming with milk in a steading, in the spring season, when the milk wets the vessels;
sentences.n: A second comparison, of the crowd round Sarpedon to flies round milk. οἳ δ’ are the fighters, and ὁμίλεον is the imperfect of ὁμιλέω, here ‘throng’. ὡς ὅτε with the subjunctive βρομέωσι is ‘as when they buzz’ (βρομέω ‘buzz’). σταθμῷ ἔνι is ‘in a steading’, and περιγλαγέας … πέλλας ‘pails brimming with milk’ (πέλλα ‘milk-pail’, the adjective built on γλάγος ‘milk’). The last line is that of 2.471.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρα τοὶ περὶ νεκρὸν ὁμίλεον, οὐδέ ποτε Ζεὺς
τρέψεν ἀπὸ κρατερῆς ὑσμίνης ὄσσε φαεινώ,
sentences.tr:
hōs ara toi peri nekron homileon, oude pote Zeus
trepsen apo kraterēs hysminēs osse phaeinō,
sentences.l:
so then they around the corpse kept thronging, and never did Zeus
turn from the strong battle his two shining eyes,
sentences.i: So they thronged about the corpse, and Zeus never turned his shining eyes away from the strong battle,
sentences.n: The comparison is closed, and the scene turns to Zeus watching. τοί is the article as a pronoun, ‘they’. ὣς ἄρα picks up ὡς in 641. οὐδέ ποτε is ‘and never’, τρέψεν the unaugmented aorist of τρέπω ‘turn’, and ὄσσε φαεινώ the dual, ‘the two shining eyes’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ κατ’ αὐτοὺς αἰὲν ὅρα καὶ φράζετο θυμῷ,
πολλὰ μάλ’ ἀμφὶ φόνῳ Πατρόκλου μερμηρίζων,
sentences.tr:
alla kat’ autous aien hora kai phrazeto thymōi,
polla mal’ amphi phonōi Patroklou mermērizōn,
sentences.l:
but upon them ever he looked, and took thought in his spirit,
much indeed about the slaying of Patroclus being in doubt,
sentences.i: but kept looking at them and thinking it over in his spirit, much in doubt about the killing of Patroclus,
sentences.n: Zeus is in two minds, and the next four lines set out the two courses. ὅρα is the imperfect of ὁράω, ‘looked’, and κατ’ αὐτούς ‘at them’. φράζετο is the imperfect middle of φράζομαι ‘take thought’. μερμηρίζων is ‘being in doubt’, and ἀμφὶ φόνῳ Πατρόκλου ‘about the killing of Patroclus’, with Πατρόκλου the one who might be killed, as 648–650 show.

sentences.t:
ἢ ἤδη καὶ κεῖνον ἐνὶ κρατερῇ ὑσμίνῃ
αὐτοῦ ἐπ’ ἀντιθέῳ Σαρπηδόνι φαίδιμος Ἕκτωρ
χαλκῷ δῃώσῃ, ἀπό τ’ ὤμων τεύχε’ ἕληται,
sentences.tr:
ē ēdē kai keinon eni kraterēi hysminēi
autou ep’ antitheōi Sarpēdoni phaidimos Hektōr
chalkōi dēiōsēi, apo t’ ōmōn teuche’ helētai,
sentences.l:
whether now that man too, in the strong battle,
right there upon godlike Sarpedon, glorious Hector
should cut down with bronze, and from his shoulders take the armour,
sentences.i: whether glorious Hector should now cut that man down too with bronze, in the strong battle, right there on godlike Sarpedon, and take the armour from his shoulders,
sentences.n: The first course: that Hector kill Patroclus at once. ἢ … ἦ is ‘whether … or whether’, and the verbs δῃώσῃ and ἕληται are subjunctives of a question, ‘should he?’. κεῖνον is Patroclus, and καί ‘too’ because Sarpedon has just fallen. αὐτοῦ is the adverb ‘right there’, and ἐπ’ ἀντιθέῳ Σαρπηδόνι ‘upon godlike Sarpedon’ (ἀντίθεος ‘godlike’). δῃώσῃ is the aorist subjunctive of δηϊόω ‘cut down’, and ἀπὸ … ἕληται, the aorist subjunctive middle of αἱρέω, ‘take off’; τεύχεα are ‘armour’.

sentences.t: ἦ ἔτι καὶ πλεόνεσσιν ὀφέλλειεν πόνον αἰπύν.
sentences.tr: ē eti kai pleonessin ophelleien ponon aipyn.
sentences.l: or whether even yet for more he should increase steep toil.
sentences.i: or whether he should increase the steep toil still more, for yet more men.
sentences.n: The second course: that Zeus prolong the fight so that more men are caught in it. The subject changes to Zeus. ἦ ἔτι καί is ‘or whether still’, and ὀφέλλειεν the optative of ὀφέλλω ‘increase’. πλεόνεσσιν is the dative plural of πλείων ‘more’, with the men unnamed, and πόνον αἰπύν ‘steep toil’.

sentences.t:
ὧδε δέ οἱ φρονέοντι δοάσσατο κέρδιον εἶναι
ὄφρ’ ἠῢς θεράπων Πηληϊάδεω Ἀχιλῆος
ἐξαῦτις Τρῶάς τε καὶ Ἕκτορα χαλκοκορυστὴν
ὤσαιτο προτὶ ἄστυ, πολέων δ’ ἀπὸ θυμὸν ἕλοιτο.
sentences.tr:
hōde de hoi phroneonti doassato kerdion einai
ophr’ ēÿs therapōn Pēlēïadeō Achilēos
exautis Trōas te kai Hektora chalkokorystēn
ōsaito proti asty, poleōn d’ apo thymon heloito.
sentences.l:
And thus to him considering it seemed better to be
that the good attendant of Peleus’-son Achilles
again the Trojans and Hector, bronze-armed,
might push to the town, and from many take the life.
sentences.i: And this, as he thought it over, seemed to him the better course: that the good attendant of Peleus’ son Achilles should push the Trojans, and Hector armed in bronze, back toward the town once more, and take the life from many.
sentences.n: Zeus’ choice: Patroclus is to go on, first driving the Trojans to their town. The subject of the infinitive is the ‘good attendant’, Patroclus, who is not named. The first line is the formula of 13.458 and 14.23, with οἱ ‘to him’ (Zeus). δοάσσατο is ‘it seemed’, κέρδιον ‘better’. ὄφρα with the optative gives what seemed better: ὤσαιτο (aorist optative of ὠθέω ‘push’) and ἕλοιτο ‘might take’. ἐξαῦτις is ‘again, once more’, προτὶ ἄστυ ‘toward the town’, and πολέων the epic genitive plural of πολύς. Ἕκτορα χαλκοκορυστήν is ‘Hector armed in bronze’.

sentences.t: Ἕκτορι δὲ πρωτίστῳ ἀνάλκιδα θυμὸν ἐνῆκεν·
sentences.tr: Hektori de prōtistōi analkida thymon enēken·
sentences.l: And into Hector first of all a spirit without might he put;
sentences.i: And into Hector, first of all, he put a spirit without might;
sentences.n: The Greek does not name the subject, but it is Zeus carrying out the choice. ἐνῆκεν is the aorist of ἐνίημι ‘put into’. πρωτίστῳ is ‘first of all’, a superlative, and ἀνάλκιδα θυμόν is ‘a spirit without might’ (ἄλκη ‘might’).

sentences.t:
ἐς δίφρον δ’ ἀναβὰς φύγαδ’ ἔτραπε, κέκλετο δ’ ἄλλους
Τρῶας φευγέμεναι·
sentences.tr:
es diphron d’ anabas phygad’ etrape, kekleto d’ allous
Trōas pheugemenai·
sentences.l:
and onto the chariot having mounted, to flight he turned, and gave orders to the others,
the Trojans, to flee;
sentences.i: and he climbed into his chariot and turned to flight, and gave orders to the other Trojans to flee;
sentences.n: Hector’s flight, and the order to the rest. ἀναβάς is ‘having mounted’, and ἔτραπε the aorist of τρέπω ‘turn’, with the object (the horses, or himself) left unsaid, φύγαδ’ being ‘to flight’. κέκλετο is the reduplicated aorist middle of κέλομαι ‘order’, with φευγέμεναι, the epic infinitive of φεύγω, ‘to flee’; ἄλλους Τρῶας is ‘the other Trojans’.

sentences.t: γνῶ γὰρ Διὸς ἱρὰ τάλαντα.
sentences.tr: gnō gar Dios hira talanta.
sentences.l: for he recognised the sacred scales of Zeus.
sentences.i: for he recognised the sacred scales of Zeus.
sentences.n: The reason for Hector’s flight. γνῶ is ἔγνω, the aorist of γιγνώσκω ‘recognise’. ἱρά is ἱερά ‘sacred’, and τάλαντα ‘scales’ are the scales of Zeus (8.69). The Greek does not say what they showed.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ οὐδ’ ἴφθιμοι Λύκιοι μένον, ἀλλὰ φόβηθεν
πάντες, ἐπεὶ βασιλῆα ἴδον βεβλαμμένον ἦτορ
κείμενον ἐν νεκύων ἀγύρει·
sentences.tr:
enth’ oud’ iphthimoi Lykioi menon, alla phobēthen
pantes, epei basilēa idon beblammenon ētor
keimenon en nekyōn agyrei·
sentences.i: Then not even the mighty Lycians stayed, but all fled, when they saw their king lying in a throng of the dead, harmed in the heart;
sentences.n: The Lycians flee because they see Sarpedon lying dead. ἔνθ’ οὐδ’ is ‘then not even’, ἴφθιμοι ‘mighty’, and μένον the imperfect of μένω ‘stay’. φόβηθεν is the epic third plural of the aorist passive of φοβέω, ‘were put to flight’. ἴδον is the unaugmented aorist ‘saw’, and βασιλῆα, the accusative of βασιλεύς, is Sarpedon. βεβλαμμένον is the perfect passive participle of βλάπτω ‘harm’, with ἦτορ ‘in the heart’ an accusative of respect: struck by Patroclus’ spear where the midriff closes round the heart (16.481). κείμενον is ‘lying’, ἀγύρει ‘in a gathering, a throng’ (the dative of ἄγυρις), and νεκύων ‘of the dead’.

sentences.t:
πολέες γὰρ ἐπ’ αὐτῷ
κάππεσον, εὖτ’ ἔριδα κρατερὴν ἐτάνυσσε Κρονίων.
sentences.tr:
polees gar ep’ autōi
kappeson, eut’ erida kraterēn etanysse Kroniōn.
sentences.l:
for many upon him
fell down, when strong strife stretched the son of Cronus.
sentences.i: for many fell upon him when the son of Cronus stretched out strong strife.
sentences.n: Why there is a throng of dead on him. πολέες is the epic πολλοί ‘many’, ἐπ’ αὐτῷ ‘upon him’, and κάππεσον, for κατέπεσον, ‘fell down’. εὖτε is ‘when’, and ἐτάνυσσε the aorist of τανύω ‘stretch’; ἔριδα κρατερήν is ‘strong strife’. Κρονίων ‘the son of Cronus’ is Zeus.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ἄρ’ ἀπ’ ὤμοιιν Σαρπηδόνος ἔντε’ ἕλοντο
χάλκεα μαρμαίροντα, τὰ μὲν κοίλας ἐπὶ νῆας
δῶκε φέρειν ἑτάροισι Μενοιτίου ἄλκιμος υἱός.
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ ar’ ap’ ōmoiin Sarpēdonos ente’ helonto
chalkea marmaironta, ta men koilas epi nēas
dōke pherein hetaroisi Menoitiou alkimos huios.
sentences.l:
And they from the two shoulders of Sarpedon the gear took,
bronze, sparkling, and these to the hollow ships
gave to carry to his companions Menoetius’ sturdy son.
sentences.i: And they took the sparkling bronze gear from Sarpedon’s shoulders, and Menoetius’ sturdy son gave it to his companions to carry to the hollow ships.
sentences.n: The Achaeans strip the body, now that the Lycians have fled; they are οἳ δ’, ‘and they’. ἀπ’ ὤμοιιν is ‘from the two shoulders’, a dual. ἔντε’ is ἔντεα ‘gear’, and ἕλοντο the aorist middle of αἱρέω, ‘took for themselves’. χάλκεα ‘of bronze’ and μαρμαίροντα ‘sparkling’ go with ἔντεα. τὰ μέν is ‘these’, with no δέ after it. δῶκε φέρειν is ‘gave to carry’, and ἑτάροισι ‘to companions’ (dative plural).

sentences.t: καὶ τότ’ Ἀπόλλωνα προσέφη νεφεληγερέτα Ζεύς·
sentences.tr: kai tot’ Apollōna prosephē nephelēgereta Zeus·
sentences.l: And then cloud-gatherer Zeus addressed Apollo:
sentences.i: Then Zeus who gathers the clouds spoke to Apollo:
sentences.n: Zeus speaks to Apollo, and the lines that follow are his instructions, one imperative after another. νεφεληγερέτα ‘cloud-gatherer’ is a stock epithet of Zeus, and προσέφη ‘addressed’ is an aorist.

sentences.t:
εἰ δ’ ἄγε νῦν φίλε Φοῖβε, κελαινεφὲς αἷμα κάθηρον
ἐλθὼν ἐκ βελέων Σαρπηδόνα,
sentences.tr:
ei d’ age nyn phile Phoibe, kelainephes haima kathēron
elthōn ek beleōn Sarpēdona,
sentences.l:
“But come now, dear Phoebus, the dark-clouded blood cleanse,
going out of the missiles, Sarpedon,
sentences.i: “But come now, dear Phoebus: go out from the missiles and cleanse Sarpedon of the blood, dark as a cloud,
sentences.n: The first order: clean the body. εἰ δ’ ἄγε νῦν is ‘but come now’, and φίλε Φοῖβε ‘dear Phoebus’. κάθηρον is the aorist imperative of καθαίρω ‘cleanse’, which takes two accusatives, Σαρπηδόνα (whom) and αἷμα (what is taken off). κελαινεφές, here of blood, is ‘dark as a cloud’ (as at 4.140). ἐλθὼν ἐκ βελέων is ‘going out of the missiles’; the Greek does not say which way the movement goes, whether Apollo goes out from them or the body is to be taken out.

sentences.t:
καί μιν ἔπειτα
πολλὸν ἀπὸ πρὸ φέρων λοῦσον ποταμοῖο ῥοῇσι
χρῖσόν τ’ ἀμβροσίῃ, περὶ δ’ ἄμβροτα εἵματα ἕσσον·
sentences.tr:
kai min epeita
pollon apo pro pherōn louson potamoio rhoēisi
chrison t’ ambrosiēi, peri d’ ambrota heimata hesson·
sentences.i: and then carry him far away, wash him in the streams of a river, anoint him with ambrosia, and put deathless garments about him;
sentences.n: The rest of the care for the body, in order. φέρων is ‘carrying’, with πολλὸν ἀπὸ πρό ‘far away, forth’. λοῦσον, χρῖσον and ἕσσον are aorist imperatives, of λούω ‘wash’, χρίω ‘anoint’ and ἕννυμι ‘clothe’. ποταμοῖο ῥοῇσι is ‘in the streams of a river’, with the epic dative plural. ἀμβροσίῃ is ‘ambrosia’, the stuff of the gods, and ἄμβροτα εἵματα ‘deathless garments’; περὶ … ἕσσον is split by tmesis, ‘put about him’.

sentences.t:
πέμπε δέ μιν πομποῖσιν ἅμα κραιπνοῖσι φέρεσθαι
ὕπνῳ καὶ θανάτῳ διδυμάοσιν, οἵ ῥά μιν ὦκα
θήσουσ’ ἐν Λυκίης εὐρείης πίονι δήμῳ,
sentences.tr:
pempe de min pompoisin hama kraipnoisi pheresthai
hypnōi kai thanatōi didymaosin, hoi rha min ōka
thēsous’ en Lykiēs eureiēs pioni dēmōi,
sentences.l:
and send him with escorts, rushing ones, to be borne,
with Sleep and Death, twins, who him quickly
will set in the rich land of wide Lycia,
sentences.i: and send him to be carried with rushing escorts, with Sleep and Death, the twins, who will quickly set him down in the rich land of wide Lycia,
sentences.n: Zeus carries out what Hera advised at 16.454–457. πέμπε is ‘send’, a present imperative, and φέρεσθαι ‘to be carried’ (the middle or passive infinitive). πομποῖσιν κραιπνοῖσιν is ‘with rushing escorts’, and ὕπνῳ καὶ θανάτῳ διδυμάοσιν ‘Sleep and Death, twins’ (διδυμάοσιν, the dative plural of δίδυμος ‘twin’) stands in apposition. οἵ ῥά μιν is ‘who … him’, and θήσουσ’ is θήσουσι, the future of τίθημι ‘set’. Λυκίης εὐρείης is ‘wide Lycia’, and πίονι ‘rich’, with δήμῳ ‘land’.

sentences.t:
ἔνθά ἑ ταρχύσουσι κασίγνητοί τε ἔται τε
τύμβῳ τε στήλῃ τε·
sentences.tr:
entha he tarchysousi kasignētoi te etai te
tymbōi te stēlēi te·
sentences.l:
there his brothers and kinsmen will bury him
with a tomb and a pillar;
sentences.i: there his brothers and kinsmen will bury him with a tomb and a pillar;
sentences.n: Zeus repeats Hera’s words of 16.456–457. ἔνθα ‘there’ is Lycia, and ἑ ‘him’. ταρχύσουσι is the future of ταρχύω ‘bury’, a funeral word of unknown origin. κασίγνητοι are ‘brothers’ and ἔται ‘kinsmen’. τύμβῳ ‘with a tomb’ and στήλῃ ‘with a pillar’ are datives of means, the pillar being the upright stone set on the tomb.

sentences.t: τὸ γὰρ γέρας ἐστὶ θανόντων.
sentences.tr: to gar geras esti thanontōn.
sentences.l: for that is the prize of the dead.”
sentences.i: for that is the prize of honour that belongs to the dead.”
sentences.n: The reason for the burial, and the end of Zeus’ speech. τό is ‘that’, the burial just named. γέρας is ‘prize’, in the free English ‘prize of honour’, the share due to a person, and θανόντων is the aorist participle of θνῄσκω in the genitive plural, ‘of those who have died’. The words are those of 16.457.
